summary: The Session Peering Provisioning Framework needs a substrate protocol. Because SOAP is widely used for messaging in provisioning systems, this standards-track RFC specifies how to use SOAP to carry SPP.

eli5.summary: SPPF defines what to send. This says to send it using SOAP messages.

subtitle: How SPPF provisioning messages are wrapped in SOAP and sent over HTTPS to a peering registry.

tldr.problem: The Session Peering Provisioning Framework (RFC 7877) says what data to provision but not how to carry it, and it needs a connection-oriented, request-response, easily secured transport that works through firewalls.
tldr.mechanism: SPPP over SOAP wraps SPPF XML objects in SOAP messages defined by a WSDL, one request and one response per operation, sent over HTTP 1.1 or higher with Digest authentication and TLS.
tldr.outcome: This is the substrate that an SPPF server MUST support. Response codes are returned in the message body, and SOAP faults are not used for them.

today: RFC 7878 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the SOAP binding that the framework in RFC 7877 requires servers to support.

sections.title: Why SOAP
sections.content:
The framework in RFC 7877 is best carried by something that is connection oriented, request-response oriented, easily secured, able to pass through firewalls in a standard way, and easy to integrate into back-office systems. The client side is likely to sit in an organization's operational support systems, and the server side in a separate organization's network, so the transactions cross the Internet. The RFC concludes that SOAP and HTTP(S) suit this environment.

The document has five parts: the SOAP features used, the HTTP features used, security, the WSDL definition, and the XML Schema types that are specific to this substrate.
sections.eli5: Phone companies already know how to send standard envelopes over secure web connections, so this RFC reuses that instead of inventing a new way to send mail.

sections.title: SOAP Layering and WSDL
sections.content:
SPPP over SOAP uses SOAP mainly as a message envelope. The SOAP body holds the SPPF message, and SPPF does not rely on anything in the SOAP header. Implementations MUST use SOAP 1.2 or higher and MUST support SOAP 1.2. They SHOULD use WSDL 1.1 and MUST NOT use earlier versions.

The WSDL uses the document/literal wrapped style: each SOAP message contains a single element that wraps a structure holding all the inputs or outputs. The RFC describes six conceptual layers, from the transport protocol and message envelope down through the SOAP operation, request or response message, wrapped object and the SPPF XML types. This document defines layers 3 to 6.

SOAP faults are not used to report SPPP results. All success and error responses are the codes in Section 7.3. If a fault does occur, for example from a failure in a SOAP library, the client application should capture and handle it.
sections.eli5: Think of nested boxes: a mail truck carries an envelope, the envelope holds one form, and the form holds the actual details. This RFC defines the envelope, the form and what goes inside.

sections.title: HTTP, Authentication and Security
sections.content:
HTTP is a good fit because HTTP 1.1 persistent connections let many request and response pairs share one connection, which matters most over HTTPS where the TLS handshake is relatively slow. Implementations MUST use HTTP 1.1 or higher and SHOULD use persistent connections.

Clients and servers MUST use HTTP Digest Authentication as defined in RFC 7235 for authentication. They MUST support TLS as defined in RFC 5246 for integrity and privacy, and its use MUST follow the recommendations in RFC 7525. When servers tag human-readable messages with a language, they MUST use the XML lang attribute, and clients MAY send the HTTP Accept-Language header to state a preference.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to show a password to get in, and the whole conversation happens through a locked tunnel so nobody can read or change it on the way.

sections.title: Keys, Requests and Responses
sections.content:
Object keys are made concrete here. The generic key has rant, name and type, where the type is one of SedGrp, DestGrp, SedRec or EgrRte. The type is needed because a Destination Group and a SED Group can share a name under the same Registrant. A Public Identifier key holds rant and exactly one of number, range or uri. A SED Group Offer key holds sedGrpKey and offeredTo.

Each operation has a request and response element. The Add request spppAddRequest carries an optional clientTransId, an optional minorVer and one or more obj elements. The server MUST echo the clientTransId back and does not check it for uniqueness. The response has a serverTransId that MUST be unique for that server, an overallResult code and message, and optional detailResult entries that name the object that caused an error.

The others follow the same pattern: spppDelRequest, Accept, Reject, Batch (which can mix Add, Del, Accept and Reject in one request), Get, Get SED Group Offers (a more flexible query) and spppServerStatusRequest. For Add, Delete, Accept, Reject and Batch, a conforming server MUST process elements in order, stop at the first error, and roll back what it already did ("stop and roll back").
sections.eli5: Every request is a form with a few optional boxes and a list of things to change. The reply has a ticket number and a pass-or-fail result. If anything on the list fails, everything already done is undone.

sections.title: Response Codes
sections.content:
Response codes have four digits. The first is 1 for a positive result or 2 for a negative one. The second gives the category: 0 protocol syntax, 1 implementation-specific business rule, 2 security, 3 server system. The last two digits identify the event. Some codes are overall codes returned in overallResult, others are object-level codes returned in detailResult.

Response code 2000 SHOULD be used when XML Schema validation of a request fails. Code 2001 carries the maximum number of requests the server supports in one operation. The object-level codes carry the attribute name and value that caused the problem, following the rules in RFC 7877.

The minorVer element names the minor version of the API. Together with the major version in the XML namespace it identifies the version in use. If omitted, the server assumes the latest minor version it supports for that major version. A client can learn the supported versions by sending a server status request without minorVer.
sections.eli5: The reply carries a number that tells you what happened, like a score card. The first digit says good or bad and the next says what kind of problem it was.

sections.title: The WSDL and Worked Examples
sections.content:
Section 9 contains the WSDL. Its port type lists eight operations: submitAddRqst, submitDelRqst, submitAcceptRqst, submitRejectRqst, submitBatchRqst, submitGetRqst, submitGetSedGrpOffersRqst and submitServerStatusRqst. The semantics of each operation are those defined in RFC 7877.

Section 10 gives about two dozen sample messages from a scenario with two SIP service providers and a Registry. They add Destination Groups, SED Records, SED Groups, TNs, TN ranges and prefixes, offer and accept SED Groups to enable peering, add an Egress Route, reject an offer, and then show Get, Delete and Batch requests.
sections.eli5: The RFC ends with a full instruction sheet for the system and a long list of sample forms, so builders can see exactly what a real request and reply look like.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7877 also apply. Because data flows in both directions, authenticating only the client is not enough: the client should also authenticate the server, often through the TLS certificate exchange described in RFC 2818.

The RFC points out that a TLS server may optionally request a client certificate, but that is not a requirement of this protocol. This creates a denial-of-service risk, since unauthenticated clients can consume server CPU by creating TLS sessions, and the risk grows if the server supports client-initiated renegotiation. The mitigations are to disable client-initiated renegotiation and to restrict unauthenticated access by other means, such as firewall access control lists. It also stresses that implementations need an authorization model, because this document does not specify one.
sections.eli5: The client must prove who it is, and the client must also check it is talking to the real server. The server should also not waste effort on strangers who just open lots of secure connections.
